The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"The bodies of animals may be as minute as one-tenth of a mote of dust, or as large as hundreds of thousands of millions of *yojanas*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* says:
Regarding small insects: if they are still present after three layers of filtration, one should discard the water.
If using water, one must inspect it carefully every day;
only when no insects are found should it be used, for the appearance of insects is not fixed, as they may have been absent before and appear now.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"Regarding 'insect-infested water,' this refers to what is caught by a water-strainer and what is visible to the naked eye;
if one uses such water, insects will fall [into it]."
One must not travel half a yojana without a water-strainer; if none is available, one should strain with a corner of one’s robe.
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:
not knowing that there are insects, or perceiving them as being free of insects.
If the insects are large, one may move the water with the hand to cause them to leave;
if one strains the water and sprinkles it on the ground, or instructs another person to strain it, there is no offense in any of these cases.
The twentieth precept concerns covering a roof beyond three layers.
There are four conditions:

first, acting for oneself; second, performing the act oneself or causing another to perform it while concealing it; third, not departing from the place where one can see or hear until the third section is incomplete; fourth, committing the offense once the third section is completed.
The twenty-one rules for instructing nuns.
There are four conditions:

first, not being appointed by the Saṃgha; second, assembling the community of nuns; third, preaching the Dharma and providing instruction; fourth, speaking until the words are understood and the offense is committed.
In the Vinaya, if one preaches the Dharma without being appointed by the Saṃgha, one falls into the eight points of respect;
if one does so on a day that is not [the prescribed time], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

The first three [cases] are explained in the Sūtra as occurring after the fifteenth day of the fortnight when the precepts are recited, specifically two days prior to the uposatha; those who depart on these days are said to have departed at an improper time.
However, virtue must be complete in ten aspects, and one's conduct must be widely distributed;
for now, this is merely an abbreviated method, as in the *Śānabukarma* (Revised Karmavācanā).
This concludes the twenty-second precept: "Teaching the Dharma to bhikṣuṇīs until sunset."

There are six conditions: first, being appointed by the Saṃgha; second, the assembly of nuns having gathered; third, teaching and preaching the Dharma; fourth, the arrival of evening; fifth, knowing their intention; sixth, the preaching not ceasing—[if these are met], an offense is committed.
In the Vinaya:
except when giving instruction, if one receives, recites, or asks about the scriptures, or engages in other such matters until sunset;
or, excluding a bhikṣuṇī, if one receives the scriptures from any other woman until sunset—in all these cases, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense if:
the instruction of nuns was concluded before sunset;
or if it was for anyone other than women, excluding women.
If he preaches the Dharma at a ferry crossing, a nun may listen;
if he travels together with merchants, he may preach the Dharma at night;
or if he goes to a nunnery.
If one listens because invited by another and happens to hear the teaching while there, there is no offense in any case.
This is the twenty-third precept concerning censuring those who instruct nuns.
It consists of six conditions:

First, it is a formal appointment by the Saṃgha; second, there is the sincere intention to serve the Dharma; third, there is internal jealousy or envy; fourth, the speech is for the sake of food and drink; fifth, the words are finished; sixth, the person before hears and understands.
There is no offense in the following cases:
if the matter is actually so;
or if, for the sake of making offerings, one provides instruction, recites the sūtras, receives the sūtras, or asks questions.
If it is done in jest or by mistake, there is no offense in any case.
This is the twenty-fourth precept concerning giving robes to a nun who is not a relative.
There are four conditions:
First, it must be a nun; second, she must not be a relative; third, one gives her a robe; fourth, upon her acceptance, the offense is incurred.
According to the Vinaya, except for bartering, if one gives [a robe] to a stupa, to the Buddha, or to the Sangha, there is no offense whatsoever.
The twenty-fifth precept concerning making robes for a nun who is not a relative.
An offense is established through three conditions:
first, she is a nun; second, she is not a relative; third, one proceeds to make the robe. If these are met, an offense is committed.
In the Vinaya:
for every amount cut with a knife, for every stitch sewn, and for every needle used, one falls into an offense.

Furthermore, if one puts it on and pulls it, stretches it, or irons it; if one rubs or strokes it with the hand; if one grasps a corner and pulls it to make it square and fold it properly; or if one follows along the threads and cords—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).
There is no offense if one acts for a relative nun, or for the Buddha’s stūpa or the Saṃgha, or if one washes, dyes, or repairs a garment borrowed from her and returns it to the owner.
This concludes the twenty-sixth precept concerning sitting alone with a nun in a secluded or open place.
There are four conditions:
first, it is a bhikṣuṇī; second, there is no third person present; third, they are in either a secluded or an exposed place; fourth, sitting together constitutes an offense.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
If it falls at a distance of one *zhang* in a secluded place, it is a *duṣkṛta*; at one and a half *zhang*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
at two *zhang* or more, there is no offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
Sitting in private with a nun;
or when a nun invites a bhikṣu for a meal, one nun sits with the bhikṣu while another nun goes back and forth to serve food.
For every instance of serving food and departing, there is a separate offense of falling [into a pārājika].
At that time, the bhikṣu should rise and say:
"I wish to rise.
He must not cause the other to suspect that he is acting contrary to the Dharma.
If the nun departs, there is no offense.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* (Duo-lun) states:
"When a bhikṣu sits or stays in a concealed and covered place, it is a place devoid of shame and modesty, and thus a place where sexual misconduct may be committed."
Regarding the two types of secluded places—those seen and those heard—as explained in the section on the two *aniyata* rules:
if one is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, or if one stands upright, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if the bhikṣu has a companion;
or if there is someone who knows [the situation], who is neither blind nor deaf.
If one travels past the limit and falls to the ground;
or if one is compelled by force, or faces life-threatening or *brahmacarya*-threatening dangers.
This is the twenty-seventh precept regarding making an appointment with a nun to travel together.

There are five conditions: first, she is a bhikṣuṇī; second, she has agreed to travel together; third, there is no valid reason [for separation]; fourth, they travel by the same path; fifth, they cross a boundary—then an offense is committed.
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:

There is no prior agreement; if one travels with a large group through a place of suspected danger, or if one goes there and attains safety, it does not constitute an offense against the precepts regarding life or the Brahma-faring.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"An exception is made for a nun who carries her robe across a dangerous path."
The twenty-eighth precept concerning traveling on the same boat with a bhikṣuṇī.
There are four conditions:

first, it must be a bhikṣuṇī; second, there must be a mutual agreement; third, they must travel together on the same vessel upstream or downstream; fourth, they board the boat—these constitute an offense.
In the Vinaya, except for crossing directly [by boat], if the boatman fails to ferry those traveling up or down the river, there is no offense.
The twenty-ninth precept: regarding the rule against eating food after having praised it for a nun.
There are four conditions:

There are four factors for a nun to incur an offense by praising the acquisition of food: first, knowing; second, receiving; third, obtaining through praise; and fourth, swallowing it swallow by swallow. The Vinaya states:

"Praising" refers to praising [the virtues of] dwelling in the forest (*āraṇyaka*), begging for alms (*piṇḍapātika*), and so forth up to wearing the three robes (*traicīvarika*); or praising those who are learned (*bahuśruta*), Dharma-preachers (*dharmabhāṇaka*), upholders of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*), or practitioners of meditation (*dhyāyin*).
Regarding "food," it refers to food obtained from morning until midday; for every swallow that is ingested, [the offense is incurred].
Apart from food and drink, if one receives other gifts such as robes, lamps, or oil, it is a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅).
The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* states:
"Excepting former patrons.

Even when the food has been served and the announcement for equal distribution is being made, if other bhikṣus arrive and the nun says, 'There are more bhikṣus,' and the donor says, 'Excellent,' there is no offense."
If a nun says, "These twelve dhūtas," she commits an offense of falling (pācittiya).
If she says, "Give much good food" or "Give it equally," there is no offense.
If she says, "The community of such-and-such a person is learned and energetic; one should invite the entire assembly," everyone commits an offense of falling.
If it is said that a certain leader of the assembly is diligent, and twenty people are invited on behalf of this bhikṣu;
one person is designated as the "praiser," while the others do not commit an offense.
If someone praises the food, one must not leave; rather, one should exchange it with others.
If a neighboring seatmate is filthy and impure, and one does not wish to exchange with them, one should reflect:
"The food in this bowl was intended for such-and-such a bhikṣu, whom I shall eat. In doing so, one commits no offense.
If one says, "Venerable so-and-so may always beg for food," there is no offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
If one did not know beforehand, but says at the time of eating, "Please give this food to the bhikṣu," there is no offense.
In the Vinaya, there are cases where one does not commit an offense:

if one is unaware; if the donor has previously intended [to give]; if there is no thought of proselytizing; if the nun herself acts as the donor; if the donor directs the nun to manage the matter; or if food is given without intentional proselytizing—these do not constitute an offense.
The thirtieth precept concerns making an appointment with a woman to travel together.
The full offense is the same as that for traveling with a nun.
According to the Vinaya context, even those who were Arhats (those beyond training) were nearly beaten to death when this rule was established; how much more so, then, for ordinary worldlings!
Therefore it is said: "If one walks within a single boundary inside a village, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if one did not know [the boundary], or if one had not made a prior commitment, or if one must go for the sake of safety, or due to the conditions of life or the Brahma-faring."
The thirty-first offense regarding receiving more than one meal at a single donor's place has five conditions:

first, the donor limits the offering to one meal; second, knowing this [limitation]; third, receiving more than that; fourth, having no valid reason [for doing so]; and fifth, consuming the food, which constitutes the offense.
In the Vinaya, the allowance for those who are ill refers to cases where the illness worsens after leaving that village.
There is no offense in the following circumstances:

receiving food while staying for one night; receiving food while ill; when laypeople invite a Venerable One to stay and provide food; when invited to receive food in a regular sequence; or when the water or land routes are cut off, and so forth. These do not constitute an offense.
The thirty-second precept concerning eating in succession:
the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* refers to this as "eating repeatedly," and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* is the same.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one may eat at various locations.
This is summarized into a single clear ruling: the precept against back-to-back invitations (*paṭipuggalika-pavāraṇā*).
There are five conditions [for its violation]:

First, having previously accepted five formal invitations, regardless of whether the host is a monastic or a layperson, or a relative or a non-relative; second, the food is of a nature sufficient for satiety; third, there is no valid reason, such as illness and the like; fourth, one accepts the formal meal from another host; and fifth, the offense is incurred with each swallow.
In the Vinaya, there are two kinds of invitations:
those made according to the order of the Sangha, and those made by individual invitation.
As for food, it includes rice, parched grain flour, dry rice, and thick gruel.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"When [food] first comes out of the cauldron, if it cannot form characters when drawn upon, it is not considered proper food.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says:
If one goes to a layperson's home and says, "The *ācārya* will eat at my house today," this is called making a formal invitation.
If the food has not yet been prepared and one wishes to go to another household, one should inform [the host] before departing;
if one departs without informing them and receives a formal meal at that other place, one commits two *pāyattika* offenses.
First, not informing the household where one has been invited; second, going back on an invitation.
These are largely the same as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Furthermore, the Vinaya states:
If a sick person cannot endure eating while remaining seated for the entire meal, it is permitted to eat until satisfied.
Regarding the time for giving robes: during the twelve months of the year, wherever there is an invitation for food or clothing, it is permitted to open one's back [to receive them].
If one receives many invitations on a single day, one may accept one invitation for oneself and give the others to another person, saying:
"Venerable sir, I ought to go there; I now bestow these upon you."
"If not, one commits a *pāyattika* offense for every swallow while facing the previous house;
it is meritorious (*śubha*) for every swallow while facing away from the previous house.
The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states:
If the host objects, one may not go in their stead.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*:
one may not follow the host’s meal to a second or third house; eating gradually until midday, one must not reach a fourth house.
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:

when one is ill; when robes are being distributed; when one has renounced an invitation; when the invitation is for non-food, such as porridge or cakes that are not considered "proper food" (bhojana); when the proper food is insufficient or too little; when there is no invitation at all; or when one receives food after having already finished eating—these do not constitute an offense.
The thirty-third precept concerns eating separately from the assembly.
Regarding "eating separately," according to this Vinaya text, it clarifies only the act of being invited separately, without distinguishing whether one has failed to assemble;
thus the text says:
"Please accept food from only three people; we may not eat apart from the group.
If one follows the origin story (*nidāna*), it clarifies the practice of alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*);
thus the text says:"
To gather those who are difficult to discipline, one may personally form a separate assembly.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*:
it clarifies that [the members] do not assemble within the boundary (*sīmā*).

This also clarifies that when there is a separate invitation or a separate request, there may be those who do not assemble; likewise, within the sequence of the Saṃgha, there may also be those who do not assemble.
Now, three aspects are distinguished, each clarifying the conditions for an offense and citing evidence to prove their distinctness.
First, the explanation of the sequence for the Saṃgha has seven conditions:
first, there must be a donor;
second, it must be an invitation according to the sequence of the Saṃgha.
1. The five types of proper food must be consumed within the prescribed time;
2. The four types of food constitute a formal assembly; 3.

One must know that there are virtuous bhikṣus within the boundary who have not yet eaten and thus do not assemble; 4. [The fourth point is: [One must know] that there are virtuous bhikṣus within the boundary who have not yet eaten and thus do not assemble.
Sixth, there are no conditions;
seventh, it is an offense with every swallow.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:

If a donor prepares food at two locations within the monastic boundary (sīmā), they should invite the Saṃgha to the place where the Poṣadha is held, or send a portion of the food there; it is not necessary to pass the food back and forth between the two sites.

If there is no *saṃgha-sīma* within the village boundary, and two donors each invite four or more monks to eat at their respective locations, one should strike the *ghanṭī* (bell), and each side should mutually invite one monk from the other and send one portion of food to them;
if further bhikṣus enter, this process must likewise be repeated in succession.

Alternatively, if one first makes an individual invitation and subsequently it becomes part of the monastic succession (*saṃghakrama*), yet a guest arrives and prevents entry, this constitutes such a case;
however, if there is no such prevention, then even though it was initially an individual invitation, it subsequently becomes part of the monastic succession.
The aforementioned establishment of the rule clarifies the sequence of the Saṃgha.
Regarding "begging separately," the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (Shanjian lü piposha) provides four cases:
first, four people beg together, or they beg separately without knowing one another, yet because they share the same host, they receive food at the same time; this constitutes an offense.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"If four persons each beg for food individually and happen to be together in one place, there is no fault, because they do not belong to the same household.
If they have been invited separately, one should have them perform the ritual outside the Dharma-gate; if even one person [among them] has obtained [the food], it is then called 'pure'."
If the formal ritual is not performed and there is no one within the boundary, the entire Saṃgha may still incur the offense of obstructing food that is impure.
According to this statement, it does not suffice for those within the boundary simply not to assemble;
even if they have all assembled, their fault is still established.
Therefore, the text states:
"If one separately invites four persons who sit in sequence alongside the Sangha to receive and eat food, yet does not share the same meal with the Sangha, one commits an offense at every swallow."
Based on this principle, regarding the single case of "turning by seniority" (*saṃgha-krama*), the offense is incurred only when one fails to assemble;
however, for "begging for food" (*piṇḍapāta*) or "special invitations" (*pṛthag-nimantraṇa*), the offense is incurred whether one assembles or not.
Now, to further clarify these conditions according to their respective characteristics so that people may recognize them, it is evident that transgressions occur constantly.
Regarding the initial donor:
according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, one is called a "donor" regardless of whether they are a monastic or a layperson;
this clarifies that when it concerns food for the Sangha, there is no offense of eating separately from the community (*pṛthag-bhakta*).
Therefore, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If one takes food belonging to the Saṃgha and consumes it privately for oneself, not sharing it with the Saṃgha—whether by excluding visiting monks or by failing to signal the intention—this constitutes theft of the communal property (*saṃghika*), and is not the offense of eating separately from the assembly."
This is explained in detail as in the preceding fascicle.
Second, there are three types: separate monks, separate begging, and separate invitations.
First, the separate monks are explained; these refer to the succession of the Saṃgha.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

Regarding those invited according to seniority in the Saṃgha, whether they be ordinary persons or noble ones, practitioners of meditation or reciters of sūtras, or those who assist in communal affairs—all who have left the household life for the sake of liberation—may enter the order of seniority;
the only exception being those who possess evil precepts.
If one says that the "seniority by order" refers to the sequence within the Saṃgha, it is still subsumed under the category of seniority.
Furthermore, it was not known up to what point one should be considered a senior.
The Buddha said:
Those who are at the head [of the assembly] are all called *sthaviras*.
When selecting individuals based on their dharma-attainments, one may refer to them as "meditation masters" (*dhyāna-ācārya*) and so forth; this constitutes a separate invitation.
If one says "ten meditation masters," then the *dharmācāryas* and *vinayācāryas* are excluded.
Because they are distinguished and selected as distinct [from the general assembly],
they are not termed "succession of monks" (*saṃghakrama*). In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Śraddhākaravarman-sūtra*,

it is stated that if one invites a person using the methods for an Arhat without mentioning their name, it is still termed a "separate invitation" (*pratyeka-nimantraṇa*), and is censured by the Buddha.
As in the section on "Invitations" (*nimantraṇa*),
the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"If a donor makes a long-term invitation to a bhikṣu, or establishes a limit of days;"
First, invite people according to one's preference and have each take their place.
On the day of the initial assembly, if there are no prior special invitations and everything is unobstructed, it is most excellent and beyond reproach;
if it cannot be made unobstructed, one should strike the *ghanṭī*.
Once the assembly of monks has gathered, those who were previously invited by individual invitation should remain in one place.
The monk who exhorts [the donor], whether he be a patron or otherwise, should stand on a high place and cry out in a loud voice: "Those with sixty years of seniority enter;
whether they be many or few, if even one person is obtained, it is called 'pure'."
This continues until the announcement is made at the end of the summer retreat; even if there are no novices or others present, it is still termed "pure.
If the announcement is not made on the first day, it should be made every day according to the procedure for the first day.
If the proclamation is made on the first day, whether the prohibition is subsequently lifted or not, there is no fault whatsoever.

If these two methods are not performed, and at the time of eating there is even a single bhikṣu within the boundary who has been prohibited, the entire Saṃgha incurs the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
If there are no bhikṣus within the boundary, there may be an obstruction regarding the impurity of food.
In the case of an invitation for ninety days, or a long-term invitation, it is as declared on the first day.

When the ninety-day summer retreat has concluded, if a donor provides further offerings for an additional month or half-month, one should simply recite the previous *dharmadeśanā* (proclamation) as a purification; it is not necessary to recite it again.
Regarding bedding and furniture in the monastic quarters, at the conclusion of the ninety-day period, they must be announced for redistribution every day; failure to do so constitutes an offense.
If a donor prepares food within the boundaries of the monastery and the hall is insufficient to accommodate everyone, it is permissible for those who go out in succession to eat in another location.
If there are two locations within a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If food is offered at both locations on the same day, there is no fault regarding the place where the *poṣadha* is held.

However, if at the location where the *poṣadha* is not held, one does not invite a person from the *poṣadha* site, nor sends a portion of the food, the monks [of that site] commit an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*)."

If a donor separately invites four monks from the monastic order to enter the boundary of the *poṣadha* for a meal, or brings food into the boundary to invite individual bhikṣus, they should instead invite one monk from the monastic order to the place where the *poṣadha* is being held;
the same applies if there are two or three locations.
At their own location, it is not necessary to repeatedly select individuals to send food to others.
Once the invited person has sent the food, if there is another bhikṣu outside who obstructs [the donor] and prevents the food from being given, one commits an offense of downfall (pācittiya).
If this is not the case, three or fewer persons may eat separately in different locations.
If one has intended to invite a member of the Sangha but suddenly forgets to do so, one should set aside a portion of food at the head of the seat of the presiding elder and send it to that monk.
If the boundaries of the road are distant, one should first take food and proceed in succession.

If within the boundary of a village, even if there is no formal monastic boundary (*sīmā*), should two donors invite four or more monks to eat at two separate locations, they ought to strike the *gandi*.
If they mutually refer to one another as "a single person" and each sends a portion of food [to that same person], it is a transgression;
this applies even if there is only one other bhikṣu who should have been included.
If they do not mutually invite and send food [to all present], they all fall into an offense.
If one prevents [a guest] from being given food to even a single person, one also falls into an offense.

Suppose one wishes to act according to the Dharma in a certain place: one should discreetly ascertain whether there are monks in the village or not; if there is no doubt [regarding their presence], one may proceed.
If this is not the case, one should strike the *ghanṭī*;
if one does not strike it, knowing that there is at least one person who has not come to eat, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one strikes it while being uncertain, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not harbor doubt, or if one strikes the *gandi* regardless of whether [other monks] are present or not, there is no offense in any case.
Alternatively, if a guest monk has been invited according to the seniority of the assembly, and he is barred from entering, this constitutes a separate gathering (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

Or, if one has previously invited [a specific person] separately, and a visiting bhikṣu arrives, the resident bhikṣus should not obstruct him from teaching; he shall immediately take his place in the monastic succession.
If they cannot avoid obstructing him, they may even proceed by announcing that a single person is to enter, and so forth.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"Regarding the four cases of separate begging:
either four people beg at the same time, or they beg individually, each unaware of the others."
If they share the same host and go at the same time to receive food, it is an offense.
If they each go separately but receive the food at the same time and eat in different places, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there is no offense of falling (pācittiya).
If three [monks] each go separately, each receives separately, and each eats separately, there is no offense.
Fourth, if they beg separately and go separately, but receive and eat at the same time, there is an offense.
The commentary states:

Regarding invitations by turn among the Sangha, once a person has arrived at the donor's house, if there is a bhikṣu outside the gate who is not permitted to enter the boundary, it becomes a separate invitation (*pṛthag-bhakta*).
Furthermore, if no one is present at the time of the afternoon meal, one also commits an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).

If the monks outside the gate are more than sixty-three paces away from those inside the house, then at the time of the meal, those outside monks are termed a "separate invitation for a separate assembly," and are not termed a "separate assembly by turn of the monastic order."
Regarding the formation of a *saṃgha* through the four types of food-offerings, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"It is required that four individuals be invited separately; when they all accept [the invitation], a *saṃgha* is formed."
If, while at the same seat, one bhikṣu covers his bowl and does not eat, waiting until the other three have finished eating before he eats alone, there is no offense.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
if there are two or three people, they may eat as they please.
If there are four people, they should divide into two groups and enter for meals alternately.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:
"If there are three bhikṣus, one of whom has a deranged mind;"
Regarding three bhikṣus: one is subject to *pravāsanīya* (banishment).
If three bhikṣus are within the boundary (*sīmā*) and one is outside the boundary;
or if two are banished while being insane—these do not count toward the number of the Saṃgha, and thus even with four, the quorum is not achieved.
Those from different realms do not count toward the quorum, nor do they constitute a separate assembly.
Therefore, one must know who is a qualified bhikṣu.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* (Duo-lun) states:

Whether eating monastic food or food offered by a donor, if each person takes their own portion and eats—whether at separate locations or in one place—even with four or more people, there is no offense of eating in a group apart from the community.
If four individuals each beg for alms separately and eat together at one location, there is likewise no offense of eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
Regarding the formulation of the offense in the Vinaya, it refers to the case where they beg from a single household together and receive food simultaneously as a group of four.
If each person must receive their own portion from the beginning and the end, it is permissible, as one is merely eating one's own food.
Furthermore, there are four cases:
first, if the host is one and all gather together, there is no fault.
If two groups eat together in one place, they differ only in their respective identities; because the taste of the food is the same, there is no offense.
However, if there are other bhikṣus within the boundary, both groups commit the offense.

Regarding the third case, the distinction of place is as follows: Suppose the entire Sangha has finished eating their own food, and there is a donor who wishes to offer a meal. A certain patron separately invites four individuals to sit together with the Sangha to receive the food; because they do not share the same status as the Sangha, they commit an offense with every swallow.

If those four individuals first take a single mouthful from within the Sangha’s portion and subsequently receive more, there is no offense. This refers to an open space where one must be within arm's reach [of the others]; if it is a covered place, it is not necessary for them to be in physical contact.

The fourth refers to the distinction of food and the distinction of location: if two groups, one from each side, mutually invite a person from the other and mutually send a portion of food to them, and if this is not done, both parties commit a *pāyattika* offense.
The five classes [of persons] do not fully assemble within [the boundary].
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If the Bhikṣu-saṃgha is invited, a Bhikṣu or a Śrāmaṇera should go."
If the two assemblies of monks are invited, the five groups of practitioners should attend.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Whenever there is a meal for a separate group, it must take place within the boundary."
Regarding the term "boundary" (*sīmā*): it refers to the boundary established by the Sangha, the village boundary, the household boundary, and the wilderness boundary of one *krośa*.
Within these various boundaries, one must not eat separately or perform the *poṣadha* ceremony separately.
If the Sangha has finished eating and visiting bhikṣus arrive, and a donor provides food for four or more people, there is no offense;
because the Sangha has already finished its meal, they do not share the same communal flavor, and thus there is no fault of causing division.
If the Sangha has not yet eaten and a guest enters the boundary to receive food from a donor, each swallow constitutes an offense of *pṛthag-varga* (separate group).

There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or a monk who has been expelled; as for śrāmaṇeras and the other three types [of persons], they do not constitute a separate group. However, if one does not provide food to the Sangha, this constitutes theft of the communal property (*saṃghika*).

If a śrāmaṇera is invited as part of the monastic succession (saṃgha-krama), one is exempt from the offense of a separate assembly (bhedasaṃgha) involving four or more bhikṣus, because both are fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
The various Vinayas, including the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, all state that the offense is committed by inviting separately and begging separately; they do not mention the condition of not assembling.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Individual invitations and individual begging are as prescribed by the Vinaya; furthermore, it includes not assembling at the place where food is served.
Even if one has come according to the monastic order, if one does not assemble with those within the same boundary, this is also called 'a separate assembly' (*pṛthaggaṇa*), as listed above."
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that there are five types of "sufficient" [conditions] for not committing the fourth offense.
First, the "sufficient by not being invited":

Suppose a donor separately invites four persons, but one does not go. Seeing that the number is insufficient, the host sees a bhikṣu approaching at midday and immediately calls him to eat; this is called "monastic succession" (*saṃgha-krama*) where there is no intentional discrimination.
Second, there were four including one who went for alms;
because of a separate invitation, one person did not go, but when the bhikṣu who had gone for alms arrived at midday, food was given to him according to his rank.
Third, there were four including a śrāmaṇera.
The four bowl-stands suffice for four separate invitations; three people arrived in person, while one was invited by means of a bowl.
The five sick persons suffice for four; these are called "the insane and the deluded."
One may eat without being part of the assembly.
According to the Vinaya, there are seven exceptions where no offense is committed:
first, when one is ill, even down to the point where the heels have cracked.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"If sand and soil enter [the robe], one cannot walk [in it].
Second, regarding the time of making robes:
After the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded, there is a period of one month if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread; if it has been spread, the period is five months.
Regarding the three occasions for the distribution of robes (*cīvara-dāna-kāla*):

as previously explained under the precept concerning "refusing invitations" (*pratyākhyāna*), these refer to the two instances of travel by land and by boat, which constitute four or five conditions; this includes all coming and going within a distance of half a *yojana*.
Regarding the gathering of the six great assemblies:
when there are four people eating, the addition of one more person becomes a source of trouble;

this continues up to a hundred people, where the addition of one more person becomes a source of trouble. This refers to times of scarcity, when two households, one to the east and one to the west, each provide food offerings; the eastern household completes the assembly, while the western household has only one person.
Regarding the formation of a quorum at the place where white food is served: there was one person from the western house who originally suffered from a separate ailment;
he was present during times of abundance, but because of scarcity, this rule was relaxed.
Furthermore, as the provisions were limited, it was not permitted to distribute them separately.
Alms from outside are difficult to obtain; it was because of such scarcity that [the practice of] establishing [monasteries] was permitted.
Now, when offerings are prepared in the capital, there are frequently monks who do not follow their official registers, crowding at the gates;
invited households refuse to open their doors and will not allow them to enter at will.
Virtuous and eminent masters sit peacefully while eating, unaware that monks are outside and failing to send for them.
Having personally witnessed such matters, I find them deeply vulgar and base;
I hope that all practitioners will restrain themselves upon seeing or hearing of this.
The *Wugong* states:
"If there is a visiting bhikṣu outside the gate who is not permitted to enter, one should even send word for him to go to his own monastery to fetch food," and so forth,
as detailed in the "Rules for Invitations" (*Qingfa*).
Seventh, regarding the giving of food to śramaṇas:
this refers to those who have left the household life outside the community of these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya.
Furthermore, according to the treatise, there is no offense when giving in the order of the saṃgha.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are nine conditions in total regarding the time for robes.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states:
The householder Siṃha invited five hundred arhats separately; the Buddha said:
"One does not know which single person among the ranks of the Sangha it may be, yet their merit is immeasurable.
It is like saying that when one drinks from the great ocean, one drinks from all its tributary streams.
The Lion then said:
"From this day forward, you shall not offer separate invitations.
The Buddha said:
"I, too, do not permit separate offerings, for they bring no merit."
The Lion then practiced impartial giving, making no distinction between those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them.
The Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent!"
Giving with impartiality yields immeasurable merit;
the giver who acts with impartiality is the foremost among all givers.
This is the same principle as that in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, where one offered cotton cloth to the Buddha, and the Buddha passed it on to the Sangha.

Even if the Dharma is about to perish in the future, and there are bhikṣus who keep wives and harbor children—groups of four or more who bear the name of the Saṃgha—one should invite them for offerings and regard them with respect as one would Śāriputra and others.
The Vinaya clarifies the circumstances under which exceptions are permitted; regarding the "monastic order" (saṃgha-krama), this single category brings benefit to both oneself and others.

As for various circumstances such as illness, these can only bring benefit to oneself—namely, when one makes a separate invitation to three individuals. If one of those three falls ill or is traveling due to other causes, they are included in the aforementioned number.
While one’s own situation constitutes an exception that brings benefit, the other person commits the offense of a separate assembly (pṛthag-jana-saṃgha).
If there are none of the aforementioned circumstances in the Vinaya, one should immediately make a formal announcement (*jñapti*), saying:
"I have no cause or reason for this separate meal; I now wish to depart."
The same applies to others who have no such reason.
If one has a reason for entering while the group is eating separately and wishes to enter, they should announce:
"I have a reason for entering while the group is eating separately."
Having made the announcement, one should enter in due order.
If one fails to announce because of some circumstance, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in cases where an exception has been granted as stated above.
The thirty-fourth precept regarding taking food from a woman returning home or a merchant has five conditions:

first, the two aforementioned conditions; second, knowing it is such [food]; third, having no other reason [for receiving it]; fourth, taking more than three bowls; and fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as one steps outside the door.
The thirty-fifth precept regarding eating after having finished one's meal has five conditions:

first, the food must be sufficient to satisfy; second, one must know that the portion is sufficient; third, one must abandon the formal posture; and fourth, there must be no valid reason [to continue].
Regarding the offense of eating at the fifth watch:

In the Vinaya, if it consists of rice, parched grain, or dry rice, these are considered "proper food" (*bhojana*); because they are capable of providing full satisfaction, they are termed "sufficient food" (*paryāpta-bhakta*).
There are five conditions [for this offense]:
First, one knows that this food arises from causes such as rice and so forth; this is right concentration.
Second, one knows it has been brought and knows it was brought for oneself; the object is generally sufficient.
Third, one knows the restriction: knowing that the food before one is small, even if one eats it, there is no restriction regarding what follows.
If one can be satiated by much, even eating a single mouthful must be followed by restraint.
Fourth, knowing the majestic deportment means knowing the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—because each instance of their impairment constitutes a full offense.

Fifth, knowing the relinquishing of deportment: if one is eating while seated on a chair and the food before one is sufficient, yet one suddenly lowers the head to take more from behind, this constitutes the case of "separating from the seat.

Once the meal is finished and one has relinquished deportment, if one does not perform the *kṛta-śeṣa-dharma* (the rite for leftover food), then should one obtain and eat subsequent food—whether it be fresh or stale, or consisting of branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, fine or unground flour-cakes, oil, honey, and so forth—if even a single grain enters the mouth, for every swallow, one commits an offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Abandoning the deportments" refers to the eight types of deportment: walking, standing, sitting, lying down, using a long bed, using a short bed, being on a boat, and riding in a vehicle.

Furthermore, for example, once you have sat upon the bed, if you see a teacher, a monk, a stupa, or a statue behind you, you should turn your body to avoid them while sitting; however, you must not drag your body off the bed, for to leave it would be called abandoning one's dignified deportment.
If it rains while one is eating, one should hold an umbrella over oneself;
if there is none, one should fold up the bed and carry it to a covered place.
If, while carrying it, the bed falls to the ground or for other reasons it is moved from its original location, and one continues to eat, it constitutes an offense of *pāyattika*.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* sets forth five matters:

first, there is food; second, its offering; third, its acceptance and consumption; fourth, not accepting further benefit; and fifth, the present-day practice where some, having accepted their formal meal and already consumed one mouthful less than required, claim they have not formed the resolve to abstain, and thus before midday, they consume more according to custom.

This is not an authoritative measure; there is no end to one's hunger when eating, and an offense is determined based on the object. When the five parts of the body have left their original position, one incurs the downfall of *pācittiya* upon further eating.
Since there was no rice gruel in the country, the drinking of flour-mash (*saktu-pāna*) was permitted at dawn.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, among the five types [of food], "parched grain" (*bài*) refers to dry rice; the rest are the same as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
As for the five "resembling foods," they are parched millet, parched wheat, wild grass seeds, mixed wheat, and *kāśa* grass, etc.
The five kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods) are:
first, roots; second, stalks; third, leaves; fourth, ground foods such as rice, large and small wheat, and so forth; and fifth, fruits.
The five *bhojana* (soft foods) in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* are the same as these.
Regarding the five kinds of mixed *khaḍaniya* (hard foods), as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"Khaḍaniya refers to branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and finely ground powders.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
One may make cakes, ghee, oil, and *modaka* from large or small wheat, rice, or beans;
all such preparations are considered "cakes," with the exception of meat.
Other items do not constitute a separate group, as they may be consumed in full satisfaction at various locations.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"Khajjaka" refers to all kinds of fruits.
"Principal food" (*bhojana*) refers to rice, wheat, and parched grain made into porridge.
If rice porridge forms characters when it first comes out of the cauldron, one must not eat it;
the same applies if rice mixed with medicine is used to make porridge.
If there is little cooked rice and much water added such that one’s deportment is compromised, one should perform the *śeṣa-bhakta-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food).
Even if there is as much as a mustard seed of rice mixed with meat, one must perform the *kṛtāvadhi* (the ritual for leftover food).
If one makes a meal from all kinds of grass roots or tree seeds, or if one makes a meal from beans, it is not necessary to perform the *kṛtāvadhi*.

If one uses vegetables mixed with either proper or improper ingredients to make congee, if one speaks of it by its proper name, it constitutes a prohibition; if one does not speak of it by its proper name, it does not constitute a prohibition.
The meaning is this:
"sufficient" refers to the sufficiency of the object before one, not to the act of eating until fullness being called "sufficient."
Therefore, in the Vinaya:

"At one time, there was a bhikṣu who, seeing an elder approaching, if he had received food without performing the *atiriktabhojana-vidhi* (the rule for leftover food), would say: 'I have received this without performing the *atiriktabhojana-vidhi*,' and then he was permitted to eat."
The same applies to nuns regarding the precepts on not showing disrespect to monks;
thus, one should know that if [the meal] is finished, the *yūṣa-vidhi* (procedure for leftover food) must be performed.
Since the preceding portion was sufficient, one may not rise abruptly, let alone in the case of the eight prohibitions in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"Regarding the leavings of a sick person, it is not necessary to perform the *kṛtāvadāna* (the ritual of 'made-to-be-eaten') again.
In the *Samantapāsādikā* and the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, it is stated that regarding the leavings of a sick person, whether they have been eaten or not, they both constitute "leavings" (*ucchista*).
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when one person performs the ritual action, all others obtain its benefit; this Vinaya is likewise.
Within the Vinaya, both monastics and laypeople may add the ritual designation to the two types of food.
If one performs the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhaktavidhi* (the ritual for leftover food), there are fifteen points of distinction.
Among these, there are three requirements:
first, it must be a *bhikṣu*.
Second, one has already finished eating, excluding cases where the meal was improper or insufficient;
third, the body is healthy and harmonious, excluding cases of illness.
According to the Abhidharma, there are likewise three [conditions]:
First, it is during a time of abundance;
second, the person addressed is a bhikṣu;
third, the individual has not yet finished eating.
The substance of food is also threefold:
first, timely food and pure food; according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, impure food does not constitute [the fulfillment of] the ritual act;
second, freshly prepared pure food that is not the remains of one who is ill.
Third, the practice of not concealing food.
One should perform three acts oneself:
first, the presence of one’s own confession; having received [the food] from a lay attendant, one should kneel together with a bhikṣu who has not yet finished his meal and say:
"Venerable Sir!
I have finished my meal; knowing this and seeing this, I perform the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā* (the rite of leftover food).
Second, one gives it to the person before; third, one extends the hand until it reaches [the other].
He performed three actions:
first, he accepted it as food;
second, he said with his mouth, "I shall stop; you take this and eat it."
Three times it is given to another.
These five types are all based on the Vinaya texts.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Buddha said:
Placing the food in the bowl, holding it with his hands, baring his right shoulder, and kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he speaks these words:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, [name], have finished eating."
The rest is as above.
If one does not eat at all, one should return it and say:
"This is my leavings; I give them to you, and they are likewise called leavings."
The Bhikṣuṇīs possess the rule regarding leftover food (*vighasa-dharma*).
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
if one performs the ritual with a bowl or a vessel, one may eat only from within that bowl.
What remains in a *pātra* constitutes a remnant, whereas what remains in a bowl does not.
The meaning is this:

suppose there is someone who has not yet finished eating their rice; if one calls another who has already eaten their fill and gives them food, saying, "This is my remnant," it is permissible and does not constitute an offense.

If one forcibly urges [another] to eat without declaring it "leftover," one commits the subsequent offense. According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases: if one perceives food as non-food;

if one has not received the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā* (the ritual for leftover food); if it is non-food and the ritual is not performed; if one is ill and the ritual is not performed; if it is the leftovers of a sick person and the ritual is not performed; or if the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā* has already been performed—in all such cases, there is no offense.
The twenty-sixth precept: Exhorting another to eat more than they need.
This involves five conditions:

first, the other person has already finished eating; second, one knows this; third, one speaks words of forceful exhortation; fourth, the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) ritual has not been performed; and fifth, the preceding person eats and thus commits an offense.
The thirty-seventh precept is the prohibition against eating at improper times.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:
"If phenomena have no temporal duration, why is it permitted to eat at the proper time and prohibited from eating at improper times as a precept?"
The answer is:
I have already explained that the names of the world are not real in terms of the Dharma; you should not raise objections to this.
Furthermore, these are the rules for establishing precepts within the Vinaya, which exist as realities within the world for the sake of restraining the reproaches of the multitude.
Furthermore, one desires to protect the Buddha-dharma so that it may endure for a long time, and to establish the ritual laws for the disciples of the Buddha.

When the World-Honored Buddha formulated the various precepts, he did not intend for them to be sought after in terms of whether they correspond to or do not correspond with specific names or categories.
If that is so, why is it said that [the Vinaya] is taught only at the time of conventional designation?
Answer:
The Vinaya of ultimate reality is not taught [at that time].
This is because laypeople and non-Buddhists are not permitted to hear it, as hearing it would give rise to false views;
furthermore, when speaking of conventional designations, it is because this [practice] applies to the majority of cases.
Now, there are those who falsely claim to study the Mahāyāna who are largely attached to eating at improper times; therefore, I have cited these precepts in full to admonish them.
The Sūtra states:
"At dawn, the various devas eat; at midday, the Buddhas of the three periods of time eat; in the late afternoon, the animals eat; and at dusk, the ghosts and spirits eat."
The Buddha established the precept for severing the causes of the six realms of existence so that practitioners may become equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* provides four interpretations:
first, from dawn until midday, as the light grows increasingly intense, it is designated as "time."
The period after midday until the light has faded is called "improper time.
From dawn until midday is the time for taking food; begging at this time does not cause distress.
After midday, the opposite should be understood to apply.
Of the three [periods], the first involves mundane human affairs, during which lustful afflictions have not yet arisen;
the middle and latter periods involve leisure and preparation, and when entering villages to beg for food, one is frequently subjected to derision and slander.
Of the four [periods], the first involves begging for food to sustain the body;
Passing the midday, one should cultivate the path by relying on meditative objects; this is not the time for begging, and is thus called "improper time" (*akāla*).
Furthermore, it is said that both day and night are each divided into nine periods, each equivalent to a *muhūrta*.
As the sun approaches its nearest point [to the earth], heat gradually diminishes and cold becomes severe, while the nights grow longer.

In the *Āgama*, the *Kāla-akāla-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Timely and the Untimely) fully elucidates the characteristics of the twenty-four half-months, which correspond to the twenty-four seasonal divisions (*qi*) measured according to secular conventions.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* instructs one to know the divisions of time; if one uses a shadow of the foot, the procedure is as described in the aforementioned sutra.
If one uses a water-clock (*ghaṭikā*), the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is likewise: when the day is at its longest, the daytime consists of eighteen *muhūrtas* and the night twelve;
during the long nights, it is the reverse.
There are four conditions:
first, it is not the proper time; second, one perceives it as not the proper time; third, it is food for the proper time; fourth, it is swallowed swallow by swallow.
The Vinaya states:
"Proper time" (*kāla*) refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until midday;
according to this time, it constitutes the rule (*dharma*), and it is the same for all four continents.
"Improper time" (*akāla*) refers to the period from midday until the dawn light has not yet appeared.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
At the time when the sun is at its zenith, it is called "time" as well as "non-time"; if one eats then, it is auspicious.
If even a single instant or the blink of an eye has passed beyond that time, eating results in a *pāyattika* offense.
The Vinaya states:
If a bhikṣu eats food at an improper time, for every swallow he commits an offense of falling (pāyattika).
If he drinks non-time-appropriate liquids after the appearance of the dawn light, or consumes seven-day medicines after the seven days have passed, he likewise commits an offense of falling.

If one consumes life-long medicines without a valid reason, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; because they have already undergone the ritual of "adding to the mouth," their consumption is not permitted when one is not ill.
There are varying degrees of gravity for such violations, all of which refer to those medicines that have undergone the ritual of "adding to the mouth.

If the ritual has not been performed, consuming the four types of medicine outside of the proper time results in a *pāyattika* offense for each; therefore, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* exempts only water and tooth-sticks from this rule.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"One may taste the food, but must not swallow it.
The *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* states:

If one instructs another to eat at improper times, to kill plants or trees, to light fires on open ground, to take up gold or silver with the hand, to dig the earth, or to consume leftover food from the previous night—whether for oneself or for another—the doer commits a *pāyattika* offense in both cases.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states:
After midday, no material object whatsoever may enter the mouth.
Once one has eaten, one must rinse the mouth with a willow branch or ash; otherwise, one commits an offense.
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:
if one prepares black honey mixed with rice, as this is the natural method;
or if one who is ill takes emetic or purgative medicine.
As the time for the meal was about to pass, he boiled barley so that the husks were not broken, strained the juice, and drank it.
If it was spit out from the throat and then swallowed again, there was no offense.
According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, if it passes the throat and is then swallowed again, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).
The thirty-eighth precept concerning eating food kept overnight has three conditions:
