if it falls upon the grass that was received as part of the portion, it should be eaten.
If soil adheres [to the food], blow it away before eating;
if there is much soil, wash the food with water and then eat it.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
The first case is when one is aware as it is lowered but unaware when it falls into the bowl;
the second is when one is unaware as it is lowered but aware when it falls.
Both of these are improper modes of conduct (anairyāpathika) and are termed "receiving food."
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
When food is being distributed, if a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) treats a bhikṣu with contempt and intentionally touches that bhikṣu’s hand, one should not accept [the food];
if they do not treat him with contempt, it is permissible to receive it.
Nine: Clarifying the Loss of the Receiving Rite.
First, loss through the intentional renunciation [of the precepts].
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states:
If a person does not require these items and resolutely abandons this food, they lose their formal undertaking (*samādāna*); to eat again would constitute an offense.
Second is the loss through the abandonment of the precepts.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states:
If one has first received food and subsequently forsaken the precepts, other bhikṣus who require it may receive it again.
There are three ways in which [the status of] food is lost:

through death, through forsaking the precepts, and through total regression. Because of this complete decline, it is like the impure eating vessels of a deceased person; they need not be turned over or cleansed of filth.
Fourth is loss through spontaneous lapse.

This refers to when the four types of medicine previously accepted have passed their time, and although the duration of the dharma has expired, there is no further acceptance [of them], as in the subsequent Vinaya.
Fifth is loss through transformation.
Just as oil is extracted from sesame seeds, fermented gruel turns into wine, wine turns into vinegar, and raw grain matures into cooked food— each losing its original character— if that were so,
why is it that in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, they are said to transform successively without losing [the nature of] the original substance?
Answer:
This means that because one applies mindfulness and awareness during the time [of the action], no fault arises afterwards;
if one does not apply mindfulness and awareness during the time, none of these will constitute a formal dharma.
Sixth is loss through contact with an impure object.
As stated in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, if a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) touches the food, one must wash one's hands and receive it again.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is likewise. Nowadays, there are those who receive [food] again without washing their hands; this constitutes a valid reception provided that no oily residue has been touched.
One merely washes the hands first with the intention of purifying the mind; it does not mean that there is actual defilement.
The tenth point is explained according to the text.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the five kinds of *pūjānīya* (soft foods) are: cooked rice, parched rice, parched grain flour, fish, and meat.
The five kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods) are as described above.
The five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods) are ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.
If one takes food for oneself and puts it into the mouth without it being offered, one commits an offense for every swallow.
If one eats at an improper time or after the seven-day limit has expired, it is also a *pāyattika*.
To eat food that has not been formally accepted for life when there is no valid reason constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
One should take pure water and a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*).
If one does not receive oil for nasal irrigation (*nasya*), and it comes out together with saliva, there is no offense for what remains.
When begging for food, if a bird picks up food or the wind blows food into one's bowl, one may remove this food—even if it is as much as a single fingernail—and there is no offense for the remainder.
The fortieth precept against seeking fine food has four conditions:

first, the fine foods consist of milk, curd, fish, and meat; second, one is not ill and cannot finish eating within a single sitting; third, one does so for one's own sake; fourth, the offense is committed upon swallowing.
In the *Jī*: "One must not beg for meat broth from a butcher;
one must likewise not [beg] from the eight kinds of dairy producers, for fear of inviting reproach and fault."
The practice of silk producers begging for raw silk is also the same as this.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states:
"To solicit fine food when not ill constitutes a grave offense."
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:

begging for oneself when ill; begging on behalf of one who is ill; begging for oneself or another in combination; or obtaining anything without having requested it. In all such instances, it is permissible to accept.
The forty-first precept: Regarding giving food to non-Buddhists. There are five conditions: first, the recipient is a non-Buddhist;

second, one knows they are a non-Buddhist; third, one gives the food oneself; fourth, it is not the case that one places the food on the ground and has someone else give it; fifth, as soon as the person receives it with their own hand, the offense is committed.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"When begging for food, one should give portions to beggars, children, dogs, and domestic animals, after first measuring out one's own share.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
If non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) seek out one's faults while giving them food, it is not called "defiling the household.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* (Duo-lun) states:
"There is no offense in giving to those who hold wrong views; if the Saṃgha gives food to non-Buddhists, there is no transgression, provided that the food is not given directly with one's own hands."
The forty-second precept concerning entering a village without informing a fellow practitioner who shares the same benefit.
There are five conditions:

first, one has previously accepted an invitation from another; because one did not accept [the current invitation], the Buddha permitted entering the village without informing [a fellow practitioner].
Second, eating before or after the proper time;
third, failing to announce one's departure;
fourth, visiting another household without a valid reason.
The fifth category of offenses concerning entry:
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu who is begging for alms arrives at a donor's house during his sequential round for food, and that donor invites him to stay, yet he proceeds to another house instead, he incurs two *pārājika*-type offenses (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*)."
As stated above regarding the section on "Declining an Invitation," by analogy with this principle,
if one person accepts an invitation and there is no one else invited together, they must inform the host family or a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) before proceeding to other activities.
First, one must not cause distress to the host by coming to inquire after their whereabouts.
That Vinaya further states:
"If two bhikṣus each accept a regular invitation, and their mutual visits are likewise [frequent], they must inform the donor."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Before the meal" refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until the time for eating;
"after the meal" refers to the period from the time for eating until midday. This is consistent with the definition of "time for eating" (*bhojana-kāla*) in the *Kāla-sūtra*.
A "household" (*kula*) refers to the dwelling place of men and women.
Regarding "other bhikṣus": they reside within the same boundary (*sīmā*) but do not share the same meal-time; because they have accepted the invitation together, the location is known.

If, after having entrusted one's bowl to another, one returns from the village midway, or goes to another house, or to the monastery’s storehouse or peripheral quarters, or enters a nunnery, or leaves the house of a layperson;
in all such cases, the previous entrustment is lost and one must entrust it to someone else again.
Otherwise, upon entering the gate, one falls into an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill;

if one has made a formal announcement (*śuklā*); during the *kārttika* month; during the season for the distribution of robes (*cīvaradānakāla*); if there is no monk to whom one has entrusted [the robe]; if one goes to another storehouse or a nunnery; or if various households have spread out many sitting mats and invited the monks.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
"If the food is insufficient or not properly prepared, seeking it from another place does not constitute an offense.
*Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*: [As stated above].
If one goes today when the host is to provide offerings tomorrow, one falls [into an offense];
the remaining cases where the host summons [the monk] are as detailed in the lower fascicle.
The forty-third precept: Regarding sitting forcefully in a dining hall.
Among the four types of nutriment, this refers to the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*);
because the visual faculty encounters visible forms, it is called the nutriment of contact.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"Men and women share food out of mutual passion.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
Because one sees forms and becomes attached to them, it is called "nutriment.
There are four conditions:
the first is the household of the eater.
The second point is as follows.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If it is a household that has renounced sexual intercourse, or a household observing the fast-day (upoṣadha), and if the man and woman mutually receive the one-day precepts (upavāsa-saṃvara), there is no offense."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one sits in a secluded place while being forceful,
those who are sitting there shall know that they are obstructing their affairs."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"In this dwelling, if many people enter and exit, there is no offense;
however, there must not be a fourth person."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"It is likewise an offense with one's mother, daughter, or sister.
Regarding the phrase "one who possesses wealth" in the Vinaya, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* says:
This is because wearing jeweled robes causes lightness and clarity, thereby giving rise to desire.
The forty-fourth precept regarding sitting with a woman in private has four conditions:
First, a laywoman; second, in a secluded place; third, in the absence of a third person; fourth, sitting within reach of one's hand from the door—these constitute an offense.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* states:
"If the door is closed and there is no pure attendant (kappiya-kāraka), it is a *pācittiya*."
If the door is opened and there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) outside, it is auspicious;
if there is a *kappiya-kāraka* inside the door, there is no offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

If there is a mother, a sister, a younger sister, or a male or female attendant (*karmadāna*) who is asleep, insane, or an infant—despite the presence of such persons, it is called "being alone" because one frequently commits offenses [in their absence]; this was already explained in detail previously, and thus it is mentioned again here.

If a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) comes and goes without interruption while performing tasks; or if the gate opens toward a road where people pass by for as long as it takes to eat a meal without ceasing; or if a lay attendant on the upper or lower gallery sees [the act] from afar—in these cases, there is no offense.
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:

when one is sitting within arm’s reach of the door so that the bhikṣu seeking alms may see them; when two bhikṣus are together as companions; when there is another person capable of identifying them nearby; or when there are circumstances of difficulty. In all such instances, it is permitted.
The forty-fifth precept: sitting alone with a woman.

There are four conditions for an offense: first, she is a laywoman; second, it is an open place where a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible) can see or hear them, yet it is a secluded spot; third, there is no third person present; and fourth, they sit together within arm’s reach. If these conditions are met, an offense is committed.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
If one sits with a woman in an open space, for every time she rises and he sits again, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If they are within one *vyāma* (fathom) of each other, it is an offense; at one and a half *vyāmas*, it is a *dukkaṭa*; beyond two *vyāmas*, there is no offense.
Regarding the non-offense concerning eating before a meal, it is as previously stated. If one mutually receives the one-day precepts (upavāsa), it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This concludes the forty-sixth rule on expelling others from a settlement.
There are four conditions [for this offense]:
First, it is a bhikṣu; second, he provides food at a specific time; third, there are no obstructing conditions; fourth, he sends [the person] away and commits the offense.
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:
providing food and then asking him to leave;
If one is ill or lacks dignified deportment such that others are displeased by the sight of them, they may personally deliver food; or if,
due to the perception of a breach of precepts, they command a *brahmacārin* or others to do so,
they may employ skillful means to send it, provided they do not harbor feelings of resentment.
The forty-seventh precept concerning the prohibition against accepting medicinal invitations for more than four months.

There are six conditions: first, the invitation for medicine; second, the limitation set by the donor; third, knowing the limit; fourth, accepting it beyond that limit; fifth, the absence of a valid reason; and sixth, the act of eating, which constitutes an offense.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
regarding the spring, summer, and winter [retreats], if one exceeds them, one commits an offense;
whether for one month or half a month, one must not exceed [the limit].
Regarding non-offenses in the Vinaya:
except for the four conditions as stated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*,
exceeding the limit for medicinal substances constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one exceeds the time limit, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is the forty-eighth precept concerning observing an army.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are three points:
First, it is for the sake of honoring the Buddha-dharma;
second, it is for the sake of extinguishing slander;
third, it is for the sake of quelling all evils and increasing wholesome dharmas.
There are four conditions:
first, a military array; second, intentionally going to view it; third, having no [other] reason; fourth, going and seeing an offense.
*The Four-Part Vinaya* states:
Regarding "arrays" (battle formations): whether they are simulated or real, all who watch fall [into sin].
If an army is ahead or behind, one must leave the road to avoid it; failure to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one employs the means of observation, one falls [into sin].
If one has been invited [elsewhere] and is unable to go due to forceful obstruction, the severance of the path, or similar circumstances, there is no offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one encounters an army and does not form an intention [to join it], there is no offense."
If one intentionally raises one's head to look out and sees [the offense] being committed, it is a *vyatikrama*.
If a celestial king emerges and one intentionally looks at him, it is a *vyatikrama*.
This applies even to looking at animals fighting or people quarreling; for one who looks, it is likewise a *vyatikrama*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Because one is contemplating impermanence, even if one contemplates [the army] in this way, there is no offense.
This concerns the forty-ninth precept regarding transgressing the time limit while within an army due to specific circumstances.
There are four conditions:
first, the condition of being invited.
The *Mahā* [Sūtra] states:

To permit those who would go forth is for the sake of the fruits of the śramaṇa, for the purpose of nurturing the Buddha-dharma, and for the purpose of increasing faith and reverence; furthermore, since the monastic and the lay communities require one another to accomplish the Buddha-dharma, it is beneficial to allow them to go forth.
Second, having already spent two nights;
third, not remaining within sight or hearing during the third night;
fourth, the offense is committed when the dawn appears.
The fiftieth precept on the prohibition against watching military engagements has four conditions:
first, being previously present at the location overnight; second, the military forces engaging in battle; third, intentionally going to watch; and fourth, seeing it, which constitutes an offense.
The precept against drinking alcohol is fifty-one.
It has three conditions:
first, the substance must be alcohol; second, there must be no circumstance of serious illness; third, the act of swallowing it constitutes an offense.
The Vinaya states:
"If one takes me as their teacher, they must not even drop grass or wood into wine to sip it from the mouth.
This was said because there are ten faults associated with alcohol.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
Because he had subdued the dragon, [Maudgalyāyana] obtained wine and became intoxicated; his robes and bowl lay scattered about.
The Buddha and Ānanda carried him to the edge of a well; the Buddha drew water himself, and Ānanda washed him.
Having put on his robes and lain down upon the bed with his head toward the Buddha, he turned over in an instant and extended his foot to trample upon the Buddha.
The Buddha assembled the Sangha and said:
"In the past he revered the Buddha; now he is unable to show reverence."
"Formerly he could subdue the venomous dragon, yet now he cannot overcome a mere frog.
Thus he spoke of the gradual prohibition of alcohol, extending even to the smelling of a wine vessel.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:
This precept is extremely grave, for it can commit four of the *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses— excluding that of causing a schism in the Sangha—
and furthermore, it can destroy all other precepts as well as other various evils.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:

If it is indeed wine—even if produced from grasses or trees—it must lack the color, fragrance, and flavor of wine; conversely, if it is not wine yet possesses the color, fragrance, and flavor of wine, it is in every case unfit for consumption.
If one cooks wine, mixes it with other substances, or consumes it as food or drink, one falls into [an offense].
If one consumes sweet vinegar-wine, fermented yeast, or dregs of wine, all constitute a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
If one drinks anything resembling wine—such as vinegar-wine, sweet wine, dregs, or yeast—that is capable of intoxicating a person, for every swallow, one commits an offense of falling (pāyattika).

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun), regarding the offense of falling for yeast: this refers to carrying dried yeast mixed with wine while traveling; other types of yeast do not constitute an offense.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

If one perceives alcohol as alcohol, or if one is in doubt, or if one does not perceive it as alcohol, yet partakes in it, one falls into an offense of taking what is not given; this refers to having previously engaged in the preparatory effort (*prayoga*).

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* establishes this rule because, fearing the onset of cold-related ailments, one might be given wine mixed with other substances and drink it without inspection; therefore, the prohibition was enacted.
However, if one inspects the substance and knows it to be non-alcoholic yet suitable for medicinal purposes, it is permitted as explained above.
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:
if one is ill and the condition does not improve through other medicines, using alcohol as medicine;
or if it is used externally to apply to a wound—in all such instances, there is no offense.
*The Five Hundred Questions*:
If a physician says that recovery is certain provided one takes the medicine mixed with [flavoring], it must not be taken empty.
To forcibly urge another to drink it when they would rather not is not a transgression; to drink it under such coercion constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
*Samantapāsādikā*:
If the medicine has been boiled with alcohol such that it retains the aroma and flavor of alcohol, one commits an offense of *dukkaṭa*;
if it does not, one may drink it.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
All fruit juices that cause intoxication constitute a *pārājika* offense;
if one eats them mixed with fermented dough or rice, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
To chew betel nut is a violation of the Vinaya.
This is the fifty-second precept concerning playing in water.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are four intentions:
First, the Buddha-dharma is revered and ought to be honored; to enter the water for sport and thereby cause damage is no small transgression.
Second, it violates dignified decorum and invites the reproach of the world.
Third, it obstructs and causes the abandonment of one's primary practice;
fourth, it leads to the loss of right mindfulness.
There are three conditions:
First, water; second, that which lacks a [specific] object; third, playing with it within the water.

In the Vinaya, "playing" refers to acting according to one's own whims and indulgence, such as drawing on the water with the hand, splashing or pouring water upon one another, or even holding water in a bowl to toy with it—all such acts constitute a *pācittiya* offense.
Once water has been removed, it is auspicious to play with fermented grain drinks or wine.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"To splash or sprinkle water and land upon one another constitutes a *vyatikrama* (transgression)."
If both [the hand and the object] are in the water, it is a *pāyattika*.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:
"To play with snow-clods or dew on the tips of grass is a *dukkaṭa*."
In the *Gāthā*: "Even for water droplets falling upon the ground, it is auspicious.
In the Vinaya, those who do not commit an offense:
If one crosses water while traveling on the road, it is not an offense to submerge in the water to retrieve sand, stones, or other objects;
likewise, if one has learned the art of swimming and floats with arms flailing and splashes the water, there is no transgression.
The fifty-third precept on pinching and poking has four conditions: first, a *bhikṣu*;
second, the intention to cause annoyance; third, the ten fingers of the hands or feet; fourth, the act of touching, which constitutes an offense immediately.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

To point at a bhikṣu with one finger constitutes a *thullaccaya*; to point with five fingers constitutes five *thullaccayas*. This applies even to designating someone by name to be excluded from a communal assembly; such acts also constitute a *pācittiya*.
If a śrāmaṇera is asleep, one should pull his robe to wake him.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*:
"If one strikes or tickles a śrāmaṇera, or even an animal, it is also auspicious."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
If one strikes or prods with anything other than [the prescribed object], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
Not acting intentionally; if one is asleep, being touched causes awakening—all these are opened up.
The fifty-fourth precept: not accepting admonition.
Five conditions:
First, one intends to perform an unrighteous act;
second, another person offers a formal admonition in accordance with the Dharma;
third, one recognizes that what one has done is wrong and that the former’s admonition is correct.
Fourth, refusing admonition and not accepting it;
fifth, committing a root offense by acting accordingly, which constitutes a *pāyattika* for violating the admonition.
This means that if one does not accept the admonition at the time it is given, one commits a *duṣkṛta*.
Subsequently, six groups [of offenses] were established, all of which constitute *pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture).
Those who do not commit an offense are exempted as specified in the concluding rules of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension).
This concludes the fifty-fifth rule of the Bhikṣu-śīla (Precepts for Monks) concerning fear.
There are five conditions:
first, a great bhikṣu;
second, the intention to cause him fear.
Third, by means of the six objects of the senses, such as forms and sounds, each is individually demonstrated and explained.
Fourth, each respective characteristic manifests.
Fifth, one commits an offense immediately upon seeing or hearing them.
Whether one asks the person in advance if they are afraid or not, all fall [into an offense].
According to the Vinaya, for one who is unclear about this, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
There is no offense in the following cases:
Or, in a dark place where there is no fire, or in a place for excrement and urine, one might mistake it for a predatory beast and become terrified;
even at the sound of footsteps or the sound of coughing and so forth, one feels fear.
If one were to point out form to others, the mind would not be afraid;
the same applies to the other sense-objects (*dhūli*).
If these characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) truly existed;

If one sees in a dream that they are about to die, will leave the monastic life, lose their possessions, or that their preceptor, parents, or others are gravely ill or have died, they should inform those individuals.
If this is done in jest or by mistake, there is no offense in any case.
The fifty-sixth precept concerning bathing more than once every half-month.
There are five conditions for an offense:

first, having already bathed previously; second, less than half a month having passed; third, there being no valid reason; fourth, bathing again; and fifth, washing even half of one’s body constitutes an offense.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Excluding the hot season— namely, the forty-five days following spring and the first month of summer—
for those who are ill, it extends even down to cases where the body emits a foul odor."
Regarding the time of performance: it includes even sweeping the ground before one's house.
Regarding the two seasons of wind and rain: it includes even a single whirlwind or a single drop of rain falling upon the body.
Regarding the time of traveling on the road: it includes even a journey of half a yojana to and fro.
All [the rules] are opened.
Regarding "none": if one falls after washing more than half the body, it is auspicious to repent through the expedient means.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun) states:
In India, the heat comes early; from the third day of the third month until the middle of the fifth month, bathing is permitted.
One should use this limit for bathing according to when it becomes hot in a particular country.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
If it rains heavily, one may stand in the open air to wash.
If there is a valid reason, it is permissible to bathe without informing other bhikṣus.
One must not share a bathing room with laypeople; however, those known to be virtuous and free from verbal faults are permitted to enter.
It is auspicious for a bhikṣu to have a layperson rub his body.
If one practicing dhūta does not allow another to rub him, it is virtuous to rub his own body with a corded brush.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
Bathing in a bathhouse together with laypeople constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika-śāstra* states:

"In general, when bathing in an exposed or covered place, it is best not to bathe together with laypeople as the treatise suggests; one must wear a *kaṣāya* (undergarment). First, one should possess a sense of shame (*hrī*); second, [bathing together] tends to arouse desire in others."
Because the body of an Arhat is soft, an ordinary person who sees it may immediately give rise to defilement and lose their male organ;
subsequently, through repentance, they regain their original form.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
If the preceptor and the patient have already bathed and their bodies are wet, there is no offense due to bathing.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
it is counted until the fifteenth day is complete.
When washing, once the preparation of the water and fire is complete, strike a wooden block to make a sound and have all the monks enter one after another in order.
If there are no other pressing matters, follow the method of a potter: first wash both thighs and both feet, and afterwards wash the head, face, waist, back, arms, elbows, chest, and armpits.
The remainder is as in the lower fascicle.
The precept on lighting a fire in an open space is fifty-seven.
There are four conditions:
First, an open space; second, one who lacks the requisite conditions; third, when grass or wood is already aflame; fourth, to ignite it constitutes an offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one kindles a fire to warm the body, and the flame reaches a height of four finger-widths, it is a *pāyattika* offense."

If one must attend to defecation or urination and returns in a brief moment without neglecting the affairs of the Sangha, there is no offense;
however, if one suspects that the return will be late, one should announce it and grant one's consent (*yadṛcchā*).
This applies even to listening to others recite or receive the scriptures—all such matters must be announced.
If one stops in the middle and speaks other words, there is no offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"When a formal act (*karmavācanā*) for settling a matter is being performed, if a śrāmaṇera is present and stands up, it is also auspicious."
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:

if one has given their consent (*chanda*) before departing; if the assembly is performing an illegal act; or if one departs without giving consent because they are acting in a way that causes harm to their teacher.
This concludes the seventy-sixth precept concerning regret after having given consent.
There are four conditions:

first, a formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed in accordance with the Dharma; second, the granting of consent (*chanda*) in accordance with the Dharma; third, the act being declared incomplete due to sudden regret; and fourth, the completion of the speech.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:
If the Saṃgha performs an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act), and at that time one lacks the power to overturn it and remains silent without rebuking it;
if one later says it is improper, there is no offense.
However, if one acts in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya [while it was being performed illegally], one falls into an offense.
To listen secretly to a dispute among the four classes of monastics in violation of the royal regulations is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is the seventy-seventh precept concerning eavesdropping.
It involves five conditions:

First, the four types of disputes arise; second, the person deliberates in secret; third, they harbor the intent to cause strife and discord; fourth, they go there to eavesdrop; fifth, upon hearing it, they immediately incur the offense without waiting to report it to others.
In the Vinaya:
If two people converse in a dark place, converse in a secluded place, or converse while walking together on a path;
if they do not snap their fingers or cough to alert one another, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if one permits it out of fear that it would result in harm.
The precept against striking a bhikṣu in anger is the seventy-eighth.
It has four conditions:
First, there is a great bhikṣu; second, he gives rise to a mind of anger; third, he forms the intention to strike; fourth, upon making contact, he commits the offense.
According to the Vinaya, one who strikes and commits a grave offense likewise falls [into a transgression].
If [a seed] falls due to the hand, a stone, a staff, or the like, or if it is struck by another door-key or the handle of a whisk, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* states:
"It is as if one were to scatter a handful of sand or beans over many bhikṣus; for each individual [seed] that falls, there is an offense."
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states:
"To strike a woman with a mind of lust constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

If wicked elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, or goats enter a stūpa or monastery and trample images, or damage flowers, fruits, or trees, one may use a staff to strike them with wood or stone to frighten them away and make them leave;
however, one must not brandish a staff at these animals, as each such act constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:
when one has an illness that requires someone to strike them;
or when one is choking on food and strikes their own back.
If one does not hear them when speaking together, one may touch them;
even if touched by mistake, there is no offense.
Examining various sūtras and vinayas, as there is no instruction for disciplinary punishment therein, it is therefore permitted for bhikṣus to administer lashes with a cane.
In Śākyamuni’s single dispensation, [the Dharma] does not exist at all; yet in the final age, it is frequently seen to exist.
As this was already clarified in the previous fascicle, this is a sign of the extinction of the Dharma.
The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states:

If monastics or laypeople should strike or break the precepts of a bhikṣu—whether he possesses the precepts or not—their sin is heavier than shedding the blood of ten thousand koṭis of Buddhas. Why is this?
Because such a person is able to show others the path of transcendence, even unto Nirvāṇa.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The formulation of precepts within the Vinaya is for the sake of worldly affairs, for the purpose of gathering the Saṃgha, and for the protection of the Buddha-dharma.
When there are persons and sentient beings, one formulates the precepts by following conventional designations (*prajñapti*), without considering the degree of future retribution.
For example, if a monastic lashes someone with a whip or kills oxen and sheep, the offense is grave while the precept is light;
whereas for praising women, the offense regarding the precept is grave, but the retribution in future lives is light, and so forth.
There are seventy-nine rules concerning the striking of bhikṣus.
The aforementioned constitutes a limit; this precept provides deep protection, such that even the mere intention constitutes an offense.
The *Gālaparipṛcchā-śāstra* states:
"If one raises a hand toward many bhikṣus, each individual case is a transgression."
The eighty-first precept concerns groundless accusation of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
it is largely identical to the second category [of offenses], with the distinction being that the offense is a *pāyattika*.
The eighty-second precept concerns entering a royal palace by force.
There are four conditions:

first, there is a Kṣatriya king; second, the king is in the same place as his consort; third, the king has not yet departed and the treasures have not yet been stored away (according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*:

the palace women are wearing jeweled robes and various ornaments, which have not yet been removed from their original places); fourth, one crosses the threshold of the royal palace gate, at which point the offense is committed.
In the Vinaya, if one enters within the threshold of the residence of a minor king of the *kṣullaka* class, a noble, or an elder, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is the precept regarding the handling of precious objects, number eighty-two;
this is clearly stated in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Taking up the "Picking Up What Was Left Behind" as the introductory narrative, the old terminology is not used here.

There are five conditions: first, it must be a valuable object belonging to oneself or another; second, it must be an item of adornment; third, it must not be located at one's own dwelling or place of lodging; fourth, there must be no intention to steal it (with the intent to return it to the owner); and fifth, the offense is committed the moment it is seized.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"If one takes hold of the seven treasures, one falls [into an offense].
The names of the seven are as listed in the thirty precepts."
If one takes what resembles jewels, copper, iron, or multicolored beads, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not take them, or if one declares them pure (*śuddha*) according to the Dharma, there is no offense.
If one picks up gold leaf or a golden image to store it away, or if one picks up another’s treasure or one’s own treasure that has been declared pure, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If it resembles a jewel and is counted among the one hundred and one items, one may possess it; there is no need to perform the ritual of "purification" (*śuddhi*).
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it states:
even for one who knows the affairs of the Buddha or the Saṃgha, if they encounter a jewel, they must not take it themselves.

If, on the eighth day of the fourth month or during times of great assemblies for making offerings, one bathes a Buddha image, a gold or silver stupa, or an image of a Bodhisattva, or makes offerings to objects coated with gold or silver, one should have a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) hold them.
If the Bodhisattva falls to the ground, the bhikṣu should assist by supporting him at a place where there is no gold or silver;
if he is smeared all over, the bhikṣu should grasp him with his hands wrapped in cloth.
When bathing a Bodhisattva adorned with gold and silver, he should have a *kappiyakāraka* (a lay attendant) wash him, and even have the *kappiyakāraka* hold him, while the bhikṣu assists.
If one has already taken hold of it, one must not let go of it later.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:
"If it resembles a jewel and is made into an ornament for a woman, taking hold of it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
Regarding male ornaments, with the exception of spears, lances, weapons, and musical instruments, there is no offense in holding any other such items.
However, if one causes a bhikṣu to hold a precious object, he also falls into an offense.

In the Vinaya, such cases are permitted as ornaments for the worship of stūpas and temples; if they are collected and secured for the sake of durability, there is no offense—this being permitted in places where no *śuddhika-puruṣa* (pure person) is available.
Thus, the *Pañcaśata-praśna* states:
"An administrator must not grasp gold, silver, or money belonging to the Buddha or the Dharma; to do so constitutes a downfall."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

"If one is within a monastery or at a place where one stays overnight, and there is treasure that one takes up oneself or instructs another to pick up, one should recognize the characteristics of the bag or the vessel;
one should open it and examine whether it is square or round, and how many are new and how many are old."
If there is someone who comes seeking [an item], one should ask for its description; if it matches, return it;
if it does not correspond, say, "I did not see such an object.
If two people come together to take it, speak to the one whose description matches, place the object before him, and let each take what they have claimed.
If one does not employ such a means, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one picks up a lost article in any other location, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
If one sees abandoned clothing or personal effects, one should announce them;
if there is no owner, hang them in a high and conspicuous place so that people may see them.
If someone comes to take them, ask where they were lost.
The answer is: it should be given to those who are associated with it.
As for that which has no owner, after it has been kept for three months, if it is found within the precincts of a stūpa, it shall be used for the stūpa;
if it is found within the precincts of the Saṃgha, it shall be used by the Saṃgha of the four quarters.

If it is a high-value object such as gold or jewels, one must not examine its characteristics in an open place; rather, having examined them in private, if there is a claimant who matches the description, one should give it to them in the presence of many people.
Instructing them to receive the Three Refuges, one says:
"The Buddha did not establish a precept that would allow [the use of] what is seen to be obtained.
Since no one has come, let it remain for three years; at the aforementioned location, it shall be used within its own boundary."
If a bhikṣu loses an object, he first forms the thought that he will retrieve it once he knows its location;
if he later finds it and takes it, there is no offense.
If a visiting bhikṣu leaves behind his robe and bowl, and the resident moves them to another place to hide them, he commits a grave offense.
If the owner of the garment comes to mind and returns to take it, there is no offense.
If one uncovers a treasure trove while digging the earth, if the attendant (kappiyakāraka) is not to be trusted, one should inform the king;
if the attendant is trustworthy, one may keep it for one or two years, after which it should be used for the construction of a stūpa.
If the king awakens and replies,
"I have already used it to build a stūpa," and if he demands it back,
one should give him an object belonging to the stūpa, or if he asks for it directly, return it to him.
If the King asks, "What does the Vinaya say? one should answer:
"The Buddha stated that whatever is obtained from the land belonging to the Sangha of a stūpa must be used for the benefit of the stūpa and the Sangha."
If there is an iron seal upon a treasure hoard bearing a name, it may be used directly; the procedure for advancing or withdrawing is as stated above.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
Some say that buried treasures belong to the king, and one who takes such an object commits the offense of theft.
The answer was:
"Only that which is upon the ground belongs to the King; that which is within the ground is not considered. Why is this so?"
Since noble ones such as Anāthapiṇḍada also accepted these items, we know there is no offense.
Furthermore, obtaining things spontaneously is not termed "robbery.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

When entering a village, one must not take any items that have been left behind; however, if someone picks them up and gives them to a bhikṣu, they may accept them, for that person is effectively the donor.
If there are items on a desolate road where no people are present, one may take them.
If a robe contains precious materials, one should step on it with the foot to break it, hold it loosely so that others may see it,
and upon reaching the dwelling, if precious materials are seen therein, entrust them to a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) to manage as the value for robes and medicine.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states:

If white robes (lay garments) have been entrusted [to a monk] and the owner does not come within the allotted time, and a layperson subsequently brings them to offer as a gift to the bhikṣu, it is improper for him to accept them;
if the owner is alive, they remain his property, but if he is dead, they belong to the Saṃgha.
The eighty-third precept: Entering a village at an improper time.

There are five conditions: first, it is an improper time; second, there is no prior announcement or invitation; third, one has not entrusted the matter to another; fourth, one approaches a layperson’s house—this includes houses within a monastery or the courtyards of pure families; fifth, the offense is incurred upon entering the gate.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If one enters a village, a monastic dwelling, or a nunnery, one must announce [one's arrival]; however, there is no offense for entering a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) or one’s own original residence.
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states:
"Improper time" refers to the period from after midday until the appearance of the morning light.
To enter a village gate without having entrusted one's affairs to a bhikṣu constitutes an offense.
However, if it concerns matters for the Saṃgha, the stūpa, the monastery, or illness, one should entrust one's affairs to a bhikṣu.
If one stays alone in a single room, one should entrust oneself to the neighboring room.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
"If there is no bhikṣu to whom one can report, one should report upon seeing [another] at a crossroads."
Furthermore, "none" refers to those who have already generated the aspiration for enlightenment.
"None" also refers to the fact that one should inform the three groups of *bhikṣuṇīs*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
Even though the meal has already concluded, it is still considered "non-time" (vikāla); one should then make a formal announcement (*jñapti*), saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I am entering the village at a non-time."
The person ahead replied, "So be it!
If the road passes through a village, and there are stūpas or deva temples within the village, one should proceed straight along the path.
If one turns left or right on a downward path, one falls.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"All the residences of laypeople are termed 'villages' (*grāma*)."
By this standard, why would one not inform [the master] regarding the quarters and courtyards of the temple attendants within the monastery?
Be cautious! Be cautious!
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one must travel along a road and stay overnight because evening has fallen, or if the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) arise, it is not necessary to announce [one's departure].
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states: "If one announces in general:"
"Whichever place one arrives at.
It is also well if one informs [the residents] individually.
If one has not informed beforehand, there is no offense provided that one informs upon seeing a bhikṣu from another monastery.
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
"If there is a necessity to enter, one must first discern the matter, namely whether one is a fellow practitioner of the pure precepts and observes correct conduct;
if one possesses the dignified deportment prescribed in the Vinaya, entry is permitted, otherwise it is not appropriate."
According to the Vinaya, there are no offenses in the following cases:

if the path passes through a village; if one has something to announce; or if one is summoned or invited—in all such instances, one may proceed directly without having made a formal entrustment (*anuparindana*).
However, if there is a matter concerning the Three Jewels, the entrustment is permitted as described above.
The eighty-fourth precept concerning bed-legs exceeding the prescribed measure has five conditions: first, it must be a bed;

second, it must be a monastic bed or one already belonging to the Saṃgha; third, the legs must exceed the prescribed length; fourth, one either makes it oneself or causes another to do so; fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as it is completed.
Regarding that which was originally intended to be cut: one commits an offense only when it has not been cut.
The Vinaya states:
"The height shall be eight fingers of the Tathāgata."
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"If a wooden bed is tall or large, one commits an offense in all cases; this applies equally to the eight precepts for laypeople.
As for 'eight fingers,' one finger is two *cun*; by the scale of King Ji Zhou, this is one foot and six *cun*, and by the Tang scale, it is slightly more than one foot and three *cun*."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one receives the gift of a high bed, one must first form the intention to cut it down [to the proper height] before accepting it;
otherwise, one commits an offense."
The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* states:
"To use a monastic bed is also an offense.
Fearing that the donor might be displeased, one should encase the legs in wooden tubes and bury them."
Even if one uses a piece of wood cut from a tree stump to prop up a bed leg, it constitutes an offense; for every time one sits down or stands up, one falls into a transgression.

If the ground is low and damp, one may use a piece of wood eight finger-widths long to prop up the legs according to this rule. For those who prop up beds on low, damp ground, it is permissible to do so if they intend to perform prostrations to the Buddha while remaining above [the ground];
however, if the bed is propped up too high, it is not appropriate.
If it concerns a high bed in a layperson's home, there is no offense; this is the same as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"Once [the bedding] has been cut, one must repent for the offense before the Saṃgha."

Regarding "eight fingers," this refers to the measurement of my own fingers used for the upper opening of the foot-supporting wood; it is measured by the human eight-finger span, with one-third of that measure inserted into the pivot-hole.
According to this principle, the commentators on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* take eight *cun* as the measure and divide it into four equal parts.
It is further stated:
A long bed is at its smallest sufficient for the seating space of four bhikṣus;
a reclining bed exceeds three cubits in length.
One may sit together with those four years younger than oneself; if one is younger than that, one must not sit together.
A bed one and a half cubits long may accommodate two people sitting together.
The supports for the bed must not exceed eight finger-widths in height.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
there is no offense if [the bedding] is eight finger-widths above the ground, or less than that, or if the legs are detached.
This concludes the eighty-fifth precept concerning the use of cotton (*tūla*) for beds and mattresses.
There are five conditions:

first, *tūla* cotton—the Vinaya states this refers to the white poplar flower, the willow flower, or the lotus stalk; second, storing it on a bed or mattress; third, for one's own use; fourth, making it oneself or having another do so; fifth, the offense is incurred upon completion.
*Pañcavargika-vinaya*: Regarding the offense of falling [into a transgression] by sitting together [with an unordained person], one must first abandon [the seat] and then repent.
This concludes the eighty-sixth precept concerning needles and tubes made of bone or ivory.
The five conditions are the same as above.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:
"Because this is a small object, it is not included among the thirty [offenses]."
Furthermore, it must be discarded because it would otherwise be subject to refutation.

If one were to return it to its original owner but they did not accept it, or if one gave it to another owner who would suffer distress, or if one brought it into the Saṃgha, it would be contrary to the Dharma; therefore, it must be destroyed and abandoned.
Regarding those cases where there is no offense according to the Vinaya:
if one uses copper, iron, lead, tin, pewter, bamboo, wood, reeds, or *śara* grass to make a needle case;

or if one makes the prongs, the ring, or the handle of a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) from ivory or horn; or if one makes the handle, the ring, or the binding of a parasol; or if one makes a sunshade hook, a tongue scraper, a *cintāmaṇi*, a toggle, a spoon, a ladle, a garment hook, eye ointment applicators, a sweat scraper, a comb, ear-pickers, meditation weights, or a nose-irrigation tube—in all such cases, there is no offense.
The eighty-seventh precept concerning oversized *niṣīdana* (sitting mats).

It is established through five conditions: first, making a sitting mat; second, it exceeds the prescribed dimensions; third, it is for one's own use; fourth, one makes it oneself or causes another to do so; fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as it is completed.
In the Vinaya:

the length is four chi of the Zhou measure, and the width is three chi; the outer border increases the length and width by one chi each. These are the fixed measurements; the rest is explained extensively according to the rules for robes.
It is further stated:
If it exceeds the prescribed measure, or if there is mutual reduction or mutual excess, whether made by oneself or caused to be made by another, one falls into an offense;
if it is not completed, yet was caused to be made by another and remains incomplete, all such cases constitute a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅).
There is no offense if it is made according to the prescribed measure, or less than the measure;
or if it is obtained from another as already completed, provided it is cut down to the proper measure.

If one makes [a robe] with two layers, there is no offense; however, regarding those who make it according to the current standard measurements, the various schools do not permit it, and it is also not permitted in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (the *Caturvargika*) during the account of the "Seven Hundred Council."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If one wishes to perform repentance, one should cut away that which exceeds the prescribed measure—meaning that which exceeds the initial measure—and provided it is not an addition, one should repent according to the Dharma.
As for the remainder, one should declare it as pure."
If ten days have already passed, one should relinquish it according to the rules for long robes (*atirekacīvara*),
following the robe regulations in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*.
This concerns the eighty-eighth precept regarding the excessive size of a wound-covering cloth (*vastra*).
The *Vinaya* states:
To cover various wounds on the body, one should wear a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*.
It may be made from expensive, fine, and soft cloth.
The length is eight chi of the Zhou standard, and the width is four chi.
Not violating [the rules] is essentially the same as the previous precepts.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
This applies up until ten days after the initial appointment; if one exceeds this limit, it constitutes a *pācittiya* offense.
The precept concerning the excessive size of rain-cloaks is number eighty-nine.
The textual characteristics are as in the [section on] the thirty [offenses]; if not understood, they may be inferred.
The ninety-first precept concerning making robes equal in measure to the Buddha’s.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:
"The Buddha’s measure is one zhang and six chi; for ordinary people, it is half of that. Both the width and length of the robe should accordingly be halved."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"It is nine spans (*vitasti*) long according to the Buddha’s measure. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* are likewise;
those versions that read "ten spans" are erroneous.
The tall women were eighteen feet in height and twelve feet in breadth;
ordinary people were nine feet or six feet tall.
Because such matters are rare, there is no leisure for extensive description; one must simply know this.
The four *pāyantika* offenses:
The first precept concerns taking food from a nun who is not a relative while in a layperson’s home.
There are five conditions [for this offense]:
1. The house of a layperson; 2. A nun who is not a relative; 3. Absence of a valid reason; 4. Taking food with one's own hand; 5. Swallowing.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"Food" refers to both that which is proper and improper.
If one is free from illness, one may take it oneself, forming a *grāsa* (mouthful) with each swallow.
The text does not distinguish between food for oneself and food for others; this applies universally based on the circumstances.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
The offense occurs in the street, but not within the house; such is the origin of the rule.
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:

receiving food from a relative nun; if one is ill; if the food is placed on the ground for one to take; if someone else hands it over; if it is given at a monastery; if it is outside the village; or if it is inside a nunnery—in all these instances, it is permissible.
The precept against biased distribution of food at a layperson's home is established through four conditions:

first, it must be a layperson’s residence; second, there must be a biased, out-of-order assignment of food; third, the assembly must accept it in silence without rebuking the act; and fourth, the offense is completed with each swallow.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"The first elder should reprove [the offender]; if they do not heed the words, even one who has recently received the precepts may do so.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
If one does not stop after the third *ha* (warning), the one who eats commits no offense.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If the Sanghas of two locations sit separately and eat separately, they must also each ask whether the formal injunction has been given; if it has not been given, one must not eat. This applies equally to those sitting later."
According to the Vinaya, there is no offense in the following cases:
if one says, "Sister, please stop for a moment; you must wait until the meal is finished";
or if the bhikṣuṇī herself acts as the donor.
If a donor provides food, they may direct a bhikṣuṇī to manage it; however,
if she does not do so intentionally but acts with partiality toward this person or that,
it constitutes an offense of receiving more than permitted from a family under training.
Rarely do matters fail to lead to confusion.
Now, even among households with faith, the five groups of practitioners frequently tread upon their thresholds and receive offerings without formal invitation.
To regulate oneself by this standard is surely a clear and decisive judgment.
There is the precept regarding receiving food in a dangerous forest hermitage (*araṇya*).
It has five conditions:
first, it must be a dangerous location in a forest hermitage; [and so forth].
Second, not having previously informed the donor;
third, being free from the conditions of illness or hardship;
fourth, taking the food with one's own hands, except when it has been placed on the ground for someone else to deliver.

Regarding the five offenses committed by swallowing food, these are essential points of decorum among the *śaikṣa* precepts; they are fully contained within the various sections [of the Vinaya], though this brief collection is nearly exhaustive.
Now, I have extracted several dozen instances that people are prone to violate, and thus I have compiled and arranged them once again.
Regarding "first, putting on the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) in a neat and orderly manner," the Vinaya states:
"That which is not neat" refers to wearing it too low at times, with the fastening belt positioned below the navel.
The "high" style has the hem raised to the knees.
The "elephant trunk" style has one front corner hanging down.
The "tāla leaf" style has two front corners hanging down.

As the Vinaya states:

The Vinaya states:
"To wrap the robe around the neck" means to gather all the corners of the robe and place them upon the shoulder.
The conditions for exemption are the same as those mentioned above.
"Covering the head" means covering it with tree leaves, fragments of material, or clothing.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill, suffering from cold, has a wound on the head, or is running while covering the head due to danger to life or to the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya).
"Jumping" refers to leaping with both feet simultaneously.
There is no offense in cases where one has an illness,
is being struck by another person, encounters thieves, predatory beasts, or thorns, or leaps over a ditch or pit in order to cross it.
Regarding squatting: whether on a bed or on the ground, it means the buttocks do not touch the earth.
There is no offense in cases where one has an illness, a wound on the buttocks, or when engaged in giving or receiving, performing a prostration, confessing, or receiving instruction.
Furthermore, "the waist" refers to the elbows being held out.
"Opening the seams" is as in the precept regarding wrapping the neck.
"Swinging the body" means walking while twisting the body from side to side.
There is no offense in the following cases:

when one is ill; when being struck by another and moving away to avoid the blow; when crossing a ditch by swaying the body to pass over it; or when adjusting one's robes to ensure they are neat and orderly.
As for "swinging the arms," it refers to swinging the arms forward and backward while walking.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill; when one is being struck by another; when one raises one's hand to ward off other circumstances; when crossing water by floating; or when using the hand to beckon a companion.
Regarding "covering the body," it refers to the body being exposed in various parts.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill, when one is bound, or when the wind blows the robe away from the body.
Regarding "looking around," it refers to looking here and there within a village.
There is no offense in the following cases:
if one is ill; if one is observing the time of day by looking at the sun; or if one runs because of difficult circumstances while seeking a way to escape.
"Silent" means there is no loud noise.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill; when one is deaf and must call out loudly to give instructions; when giving food with a loud voice; or when running at a loud voice due to the two types of danger.
"Laughing in jest" refers to laughing with the teeth exposed.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill; when the lips are painful and one does not cover the teeth; or when one smiles out of joy while recollecting the Dharma.
Regarding "eating with deliberate care," this does not mean discarding the soup or rice.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one has such an illness; if the bowl is small and one discards the food; or if the food falls back onto the table.
To receive food with a level bowl means that the bowl must not be overflowing.
One does not violate the aforementioned precepts.
Regarding receiving soup with a level bowl, this refers to when it does not overflow and drip;
one does not violate the aforementioned [precepts] in such cases.
Regarding "eating soup and rice together": this does not mean that one finishes the rice before the soup is exhausted, nor that one finishes the soup before the rice is exhausted.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill; when one specifically requires rice; when the world requires soup; when the time for the meal is about to expire; or when eating quickly due to two simultaneous difficulties.
"Eating in order" does not mean taking food from various places within the bowl and eating it.
There is no offense in cases of illness,
or when suffering from heat and picking out a cool spot, or when the day is about to end, or due to other difficult circumstances.
"Regarding not stirring the contents of the bowl": one places the food on the four sides and stirs from the center of the bowl down to the bottom.
There is no offense in cases where one has an illness, or when suffering from heat and opens the center to allow it to cool, or when the day has passed, or when there are difficult circumstances.
Seeking food for oneself.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill; when acting for another; when another acts for oneself; or when obtaining it without having sought it.
Covering the soup with rice.
There is no offense in the following cases:
if one is ill; if invited to a meal; or if one specifically requires soup or specifically requires rice.
To look at one’s neighbor in the seat means to observe who has more or less [of food].

There is no offense if the neighbor is ill or blind, or if one looks on their behalf to see whether they have received food or not, whether it is pure or impure, or whether it has been formally accepted or not; or if it is one's own self that is ill.
Regarding "the thought of food while the bowl is tied [to the waist]": this means not looking left or right.
There is no offense in cases where one has an illness, when the neighbor's seat is dark-sighted as in the previous precept, when the day has passed, or when there are difficult circumstances.
"Not taking large mouthfuls" does not mean that the mouth cannot physically accommodate them.
"Not committing an offense" refers to those who eat quickly due to illness, when the time for eating is about to pass, or because of two urgent difficulties.
"Waiting with the mouth open for rice" refers to opening one's mouth before the morsel of rice has even arrived.
One does not commit an offense in this case, as was explained in the preceding precept.
"Speaking while holding food in the mouth" means that when food remains in the mouth, speech cannot be completed clearly, causing others to fail to understand.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill; when one is choking and seeks water; when there are circumstances of difficulty;
or when food is thrown from a distance into the mouth.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill, or when being bound and food is thrown into one's mouth.
Regarding "dropped food": it is that which is half in the hand and half in the mouth.
There is no offense in eating thin pancakes, scorched rice, fruits, melons, or vegetables.
To "cheek-eat" means to cause both cheeks to bulge out like the appearance of a macaque.
There is no offense for one who is ill,
for one whose mealtime is about to pass, or for one who eats quickly due to urgent circumstances.
One must not make noise while chewing rice.
Except in cases of illness, there is no allowance for dried cakes, scorched rice, or fruits and melons; there is likewise no provision for eating vegetables.
To "sip rice" means to open one's mouth and draw in air from a distance while eating.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is ill or has a painful mouth;
or when one consumes soup, milk, curd, or bitter vinegar.
"Not licking while eating" refers to sticking out the tongue to lick up the rice.
Exceptions are when one is ill, bound, or has mud, dirt, grease, or sweat on the hands; in such cases, one may take food by licking it with the tongue.
One shakes the hand over the food:
to remove disease-causing elements, grass, or insects from the food; or to shake off any impurity on the hand;
or to shake off food that has not yet been formally received, or any filth from the hand that has touched it.
"To scatter the food" means to discard the rice.
This is explained as in the preceding precept.
"Not to hold a food vessel with soiled hands" refers to having greasy rice adhering to the hands.
Except in cases of illness, or when receiving [food] upon grass, or receiving it upon leaves, or receiving it with washed hands.
As for "washing-bowl water," this refers to water mixed with rice.
Except in cases of illness, or when receiving it in a washbasin and then discarding it.
One must not defecate or urinate upon living grass,
except when one is ill and unable to avoid it, or when [excrement] has flowed onto it, or has been dropped there by a bird.
One must not defecate, urinate, or spit into water.
Except in cases of illness, or when urine or feces flow and fall while on dry land; the rest is as in the preceding precept.
One should not stand while urinating or defecating.
Exceptions are granted for those who are ill, those who are bound, or those whose feet are soiled with grease or mud.
One must not preach the Dharma without showing respect;
however, this does not apply when one is ill, or when preaching for a king, or for a royal minister.
One must not observe the precept against staying overnight within a Buddhist stūpa.
Except when ill, for the purpose of guarding [the object], staying overnight while being held by force, or staying due to the circumstances of the two difficulties.
The precept against concealing objects within a stupa:
except when ill, for the purpose of securing it, or other difficult circumstances as mentioned above.
The precept against wearing leather sandals beneath the various stupas,
except in cases of such illness or when forcibly summoned into the stupa;
the precept against sitting beneath a stupa while leaving food behind.

except when one is ill, must travel by this path, or is forcibly summoned away;
nor [carrying] an image of the Buddha to a place for defecation or urination.
